column1: “I pay the Band A tariff and still don't get light.”
column2: That's unacceptable, and you have rights. Band A customers are entitled to at least 20 hours of supply a day. When supply fell short in early 2026, the regulator ordered distribution companies to compensate affected Band A customers. If your feeder isn't meeting 20 hours, report it.
column3: NERC Directive NERC/2026/002: compensation for Feb–Mar 2026 shortfalls, due by 31 May and 30 June 2026.

column2: I won't tell you it's fixed, because it isn't. The grid set a record of about 5,800MW in March 2025, but supply is still unreliable and outages continue. The reforms that matter most are new: states can now run their own power markets, and metering is being funded.
column3: Peak 5,801.84MW (March 2025); generation still around 4,000–5,400MW in late 2026. Never say "electricity is fixed."

column1: “Electricity tariffs keep going up for ordinary people.”
column2: The big increase in 2024 was for Band A customers, who are meant to get 20+ hours a day. Bands B to E are still priced below the real cost: the government spent about ₦1.93 trillion in 2025 keeping those tariffs down.
column3: NERC: 2025 electricity tariff subsidy obligation ₦1.93tn. Band A rose to about ₦225/kWh in April 2024.

column1: “My state can't do anything about electricity.”
column2: Actually, it now can. The Electricity Act 2023, signed by President Tinubu, lets states run their own electricity markets, licensing suppliers and setting tariffs. Fifteen states had already taken control by April 2026. It's worth asking whether yours has.
column3: NERC: 15 states with their own electricity regulators as of April 2026 (including Lagos, Enugu, Edo, Ekiti, Ondo).

column1: What is the key fact about electricity callers must accept?
column2: The universal promise to end estimated billing and meter everyone has not been met (AdvoKC rated it broken). Acknowledge it, cite the metering funds and Electricity Act, and never claim supply is fixed.
